title: The Ark, the Table, the Lampstand, and the Altar of Incense
summary: Bezalel makes the golden furnishings of the sanctuary: the ark of acacia wood overlaid with gold, the mercy seat with its two hammered-gold cherubim, the table for the bread of the Presence and its utensils, the seven-branched lampstand shaped with almond blossoms, and the incense altar. He also prepares the sacred anointing oil and the fragrant incense.
story: With the tent itself built in chapter 36, the work moves inside to the objects that will stand in God's house. These are the furnishings God described first and most carefully on the mountain (chapter 25), and now the Spirit-filled craftsman makes them. The ark in particular will carry the stone tablets of the renewed covenant, the very words the people broke with the calf and God graciously rewrote. The ark will go before Israel through the wilderness, across the Jordan, into battle, and finally into Solomon's temple; this chapter is its beginning. In chapter 38 the work moves outward again to the altar and the courtyard.
historical:
The ark was a chest about two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide and high, roughly 45 by 27 by 27 inches, small enough to be carried on poles by four men. Egypt offers the closest parallels to its form: sacred chests and shrines with carrying poles, and gods' portable boats carried by priests in procession. A gilded chest with carrying poles topped by a figure of the god Anubis was found in the tomb of Tutankhamun (fourteenth century BC), and Egyptian art often shows winged goddesses spreading protective wings over a shrine. The ark's form belonged to its world; its meaning did not, since it held no image of a god, only written words.

The ark's later history runs through Israel's story. It led the crossing of the Jordan (Joshua 3), was captured by the Philistines and returned (1 Samuel 4 to 6), was brought to Jerusalem by David (2 Samuel 6), and was placed in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8). After that it vanishes from the record. Most historians assume it was lost when the Babylonians destroyed the temple in 587 or 586 BC. The lampstand's successor in the Second Temple can still be seen carved on the Arch of Titus in Rome, carried away among the spoils after the temple fell in AD 70.
cultural:
Kings of the ancient Near East sat on thrones flanked by winged guardian figures and rested their feet on footstools, and treaties were stored at the feet of the gods who witnessed them. Israel's ark combined these ideas. The covenant tablets were kept inside it (25:16), and the cherubim above formed the throne of an invisible king. The Old Testament calls the ark God's footstool (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 132:7) and describes the LORD as enthroned between the cherubim (1 Samuel 4:4; Psalm 99:1). The empty space above the mercy seat, where other peoples would have placed a statue, was where God promised to meet Moses (25:22).

The table held twelve loaves, the bread of the Presence, renewed each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5-9), one for each tribe, set before God continually. The lampstand was a stylized almond tree in pure gold. The almond is the first tree to blossom in the land of Israel, flowering in late winter, and many interpreters see in the lampstand a picture of the tree of life, with its light burning before God through the night. A talent of gold (verse 24) is usually estimated at about 75 pounds, or 34 kilograms.
literary: The chapter follows 25:10-40 and 30:1-5 closely but moves in a clear spatial order, from the innermost object outward: the ark in the Most Holy Place, then the table, lampstand, and incense altar in the holy place. The incense altar, which in the instructions was added later in chapter 30, is now placed with the other golden furniture where it belongs. The report is shorter than the instructions because it leaves out their purpose statements. It never repeats, for example, God's promise, “I will meet with you there above the mercy seat” (25:22). The reader already knows what these things are for; here the emphasis falls on the fact that they were made, exactly and in pure gold.

outline.t: The mercy seat and the cherubim
The anointing oil and the incense

doctrines.note: The ark with its cherubim is a throne without an image. God is truly present and enthroned among his people, and yet invisible and not to be represented. The chapter holds God's nearness and his transcendence together in one object.
At the center of the sanctuary, inside the most sacred object, were the tablets of God's words. Israel's holiest place held no statue but a text. God is known first by what he says.

The golden lid of the ark, the mercy seat, was the place where blood was sprinkled once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14-15). God's law lay inside the ark, and the place of atonement covered it.

words.note: Kapporet, mercy seat or atonement cover. The word is related to kipper, to make atonement, and names the golden lid of the ark as the place where atonement was made. The English phrase mercy seat goes back to William Tyndale's translation in the 1530s. The Septuagint rendered the word hilasterion, the term Paul uses of Christ in Romans 3:25.

Aron, chest or box. The same word is used for Joseph's coffin in Genesis 50:26. It is not the word for Noah's ark, which is a different Hebrew term. The ark is usually called the ark of the Testimony or of the covenant, named for the tablets it contained.

Menorah, lampstand. The golden menorah with its seven lamps became the most lasting symbol of Jewish identity, carved on the Arch of Titus and used today in the emblem of the State of Israel. The Hanukkah lamp, with its eight branches and a helper light, is a related but distinct object.

Shaqad, to be shaped like almond blossoms. It is related to shaqed, almond tree, and to a verb meaning to watch or be wakeful. Jeremiah 1:11-12 plays on the link: Jeremiah sees an almond branch, and God says he is watching over his word to accomplish it. Aaron's staff also sprouted almonds (Numbers 17:8).

christ: Nearly every object in this chapter is taken up by the New Testament. Paul says God presented Christ as a hilasterion, the Greek word for the mercy seat, through faith in his blood (Romans 3:25), so that Jesus is both the sacrifice and the place where atonement is made. Hebrews 9:3-5 describes the ark, the jar of manna, Aaron's staff, and “the cherubim of glory, overshadowing the mercy seat,” as a pattern pointing to Christ's entrance into heaven. Jesus calls himself the bread of life (John 6:35) and says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). In Revelation 1:12-13 John sees seven golden lampstands and the risen Christ standing among them. Some readers also notice that John's Gospel places two angels in the empty tomb, one at the head and one at the feet where Jesus' body had lain (John 20:12), like the two cherubim facing each other over the mercy seat; that is a suggestive echo, not a claim John makes explicitly.

hard.q: What happened to the ark of the covenant?
hard.a:
The Bible does not say. The ark is last clearly placed in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:6-9), and 2 Chronicles 35:3 mentions it in the reign of Josiah in the late seventh century BC. When the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, the list of temple objects they carried off does not mention it (2 Kings 25:13-17). Most historians conclude that it was destroyed or taken as plunder then, or perhaps earlier. Jeremiah expected a day when no one would remember it or miss it, “nor will another one be made” (Jeremiah 3:16), which suggests he did not expect its recovery.

Later traditions filled the gap. The book of 2 Maccabees (2:4-8) tells a legend that Jeremiah hid the ark in a cave on the mountain from which Moses viewed the land. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church holds that the ark rests in a chapel at Aksum, though no outsider has been allowed to examine what is there. No evidence supports the more sensational modern claims of discovery. The New Testament's interest lies elsewhere: in the throne of God in heaven, where Revelation 11:19 glimpses the ark of his covenant in his heavenly temple.

questions: Israel's holiest object held words rather than an image. What does that suggest about how God wants to be known?
The mercy seat covered the law. How does it change your view of God's commands to know they came with a place of atonement built in?
The lampstand was designed to burn through the night before God. Where do you need to keep a light burning in a dark season?
